Sensitivity Analysis for Sample Size Planning From the AIPE Perspective for a Reliability Coefficient

Source: R/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.R
ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.Rd

Quantifies how much misspecification of the population reliability coefficient distorts an AIPE-based sample size plan for the reliability of a composite score. On each replication the function simulates an n \(\times\) J data matrix of subjects by items from a single-factor model of parallel tests whose population reliability of the sum score equals true_reliability, fits the requested estimator (alpha or omega) via the corresponding reliability_* function with the supplied ci_method, and records the realized reliability estimate and its confidence interval.

Population model. Each item has a single common-factor loading and uncorrelated unique error. With per-item variance normalized to 1, the loading and unique variance are chosen so the reliability of the sum score equals true_reliability: $$\lambda^2 \;=\; \frac{\rho}{J(1 - \rho) + \rho}, \qquad \psi^2 \;=\; 1 - \lambda^2,$$ where \(\rho = \)true_reliability and \(J\) is the number of items, n_items. Item scores are \(y_{ij} = \lambda T_i + e_{ij}\), with \(T_i \sim N(0, 1)\) and \(e_{ij} \sim N(0, \psi^2)\).

Missing data. Two arguments carry a plan into incomplete data, and they stand to each other as supposed_reliability stands to true_reliability. fmi is the planning value: the fraction of missing information the plan assumes for the coefficient, passed to ss_aipe_reliability, which enlarges the sample size accordingly. missing_prop is the data generating mechanism: each simulated item score is deleted independently with that probability (missing completely at random), and every replication is analyzed by full information maximum likelihood. A plan made with fmi is then judged by the widths the incomplete data actually deliver, and a plan that ignored the missing data (fmi = 0) is seen to fall short. Planning with fmi while simulating complete data shows the opposite misspecification, widths narrower than planned.

Usage

ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(
  true_reliability = NULL,
  supposed_reliability = NULL,
  n_items,
  width,
  specified_N = NULL,
  estimator = c("alpha", "omega"),
  ci_method = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  assurance = NULL,
  G = 1000,
  print_iter = FALSE,
  filename = NULL,
  fmi = 0,
  missing_prop = 0,
  B = NULL,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

true_reliability

Population reliability coefficient (in \([0, 1)\)).

supposed_reliability

Reliability supposed when the study is planned, a planning assumption rather than an estimate from data; the function passes the factor loading and residual variance it implies to ss_aipe_reliability as true_factor_loading and true_residual_var.

n_items

Number of items in the composite (\(J\) in the formulas): a whole number of at least 2, and at least 3 for estimator = "omega".

width

Desired full width of the CI on reliability.

specified_N

Sample size to evaluate (incompatible with supposed_reliability).

estimator

One of "alpha" (default; coefficient alpha via reliability_alpha) or "omega" (composite reliability via reliability_omega). For a population of parallel tests the two coincide; differences in sample estimates reflect estimator-specific finite-sample bias and CI behavior.

ci_method

CI method passed to the estimator. The default NULL is "ml" for alpha and omega, with complete or incomplete data: the normal theory Wald interval the plan is made for (see Details). Any other interval the estimator offers can be named.

conf_level

Confidence level (default 0.95).

assurance

Optional assurance probability passed to the planner, whose Monte Carlo search then runs at its defaults (G_initial = 500, G = 5000) and draws from the current random number stream, so set.seed() before the call makes the plan and the simulation reproducible together. The plan is the one the planner reports for the parallel model with the normal theory interval, which the default ci_method evaluates; specified_N evaluates any other size.

G

Number of Monte Carlo replications.

print_iter

Logical.

filename

Optional path for a comma separated file recording every replication (the sample reliability estimate, the two confidence limits, the interval width, and two indicators of whether the interval missed true_reliability below or above, followed, when missing_prop is above 0, by the fraction of missing information the replication realized for the coefficient): nothing is written when filename is NULL (the default), a new file with a header row is created otherwise, an existing file at that path is appended to, and a throwaway run should point it at tempfile(fileext = ".csv").

fmi

The fraction of missing information the plan assumes for the coefficient, passed to ss_aipe_reliability when supposed_reliability resolves the sample size: a single number in \([0, 1)\), with the default 0 for a complete data plan. With specified_N there is no plan for it to act on, and a value above 0 is an error.

missing_prop

The probability with which each simulated item score is missing, completely at random: a single number in \([0, 1)\). The default 0 simulates complete data; above 0, every replication is analyzed by full information maximum likelihood (see Details).

B

Number of bootstrap replications inside each simulated study when ci_method is a bootstrap method. The default, NULL, is the larger of 200 and one and a quarter times the number the interval method and the level require (see dmar_bootstrap): 500 for "percentile", 2500 for "bca", and 200 for the two bootstrap standard error methods at the 95 percent level. The quarter is room for replications that return no value (a resample without a one-factor solution): the required number (400, 2000, 100) is held to the request, so a simulated study that loses a few replications still reports its interval, and with the quarter its limits still rest on about the required number. A simulated study in which more than half of the replications return no value reports no interval. Every simulated study runs B replications, so the run time is proportional to G times B. Not used by the other interval methods.

seed

NULL (the default) to draw from the current random number stream, or a single number that makes the call reproducible; a supplied seed is set for this call only, and the caller's random number state is restored when the function returns.

Value

A data.frame with rows for mean / median / SD of the realized reliability and CI width, the proportion of intervals at or below width, tail-specific and overall non-coverage of true_reliability, and the input echoes total_N, n_items, true_reliability, supposed_reliability, width, conf_level, and assurance (present only when an assurance was supplied). The proportion of intervals at or below width, the widths, and the noncoverage proportions are over the replications that returned an interval. The simulation attribute records the numbers of replications attempted, with an interval, and without one (see the section on the record of the simulation), and, here, the message of the first failure (first_failure). When fmi or missing_prop is above 0, the rows are unchanged and the missing data inputs travel as attributes: fmi (NA with specified_N), missing_prop, and, when fmi is above 0, necessary_N_complete, the planner's complete data sample size. When missing_prop is above 0, two more attributes record the fraction of missing information the simulated data realized for the coefficient: mean_realized_fmi, its mean over the replications in which it was computed, and n_realized_fmi, the number of those replications. With fmi and missing_prop both at 0 no attribute is added. With a bootstrap ci_method the result also carries the attributes B, B_used, n_dropped, B_required, and bootstrap_status of dmar_bootstrap; they record the request each simulated study ran (B_used equals B and n_dropped is 0, because replications dropped inside a simulated study are not totaled), and bootstrap_status is "exploratory" when B is below B_required.

Details

The interval evaluated. An AIPE plan is made for a particular confidence interval procedure, so a check of the plan evaluates that procedure. The plan here is the one ss_aipe_reliability makes for the parallel model with the normal theory interval: its closed form takes the sampling variance of alpha to be the compound symmetry form \(2 (1 - \rho)^2 J / ((J - 1)(N - 1))\) of van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel (2000), and its assurance search forms, on each simulated sample, the Wald interval with that variance at the sample alpha. The default ci_method = "ml" evaluates the interval of reliability_alpha(ci_method = "ml"), the Wald interval with the general variance of van Zyl et al. at the sample covariance matrix, which at a population of parallel items is the same variance; for omega it evaluates the interval of reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"), the delta method Wald interval of the model implied omega, whose variance at a population of parallel items is that same compound symmetry form (it is the variance ss_aipe_reliability() plans with for the congeneric model, and the two agree to machine precision there). The plan does not describe other intervals, among them Bonett's (2002) for alpha and "mlr" for omega. With four items, a true and planned reliability of .80, a width of .15, and an assurance of .80, the plan of 99 cases gave alpha intervals no wider than .15 in 81.3 percent of 2,000 replications with "ml" and in 76.75 percent with Bonett's interval (set.seed(113) before each call); for omega the two intervals came closer (83.3 percent of 1,000 with "ml" and 81.9 with "mlr"). Any other interval the estimator offers can still be named in ci_method, which asks how the planned N serves an interval other than the one it was planned for.

The analysis under missing data. With missing_prop above 0, coefficient alpha is reliability_alpha(missing = "fiml"), the classical coefficient computed from the full information maximum likelihood estimate of the item covariance matrix, whose "ml" interval, the default here as with complete data, takes its standard error from the FIML information matrix of the saturated model. Coefficient omega is reliability_omega(missing = "fiml"), whose "ml" interval takes its standard error from the FIML information matrix of the single-factor model. These are the Wald intervals the planner's fmi adjustment plans for, with the standard error the missing data inflate. The complete data closed forms (Bonett, Feldt, Fisher, Hakstian-Whalen) and the asymptotic distribution-free intervals do not apply to partially observed rows, so, with missing_prop above 0, ci_method must be "ml" or "ml_logistic" for alpha and one of "ml", "mlr", "ml_logistic", or "mlr_logistic" for omega. A row that loses every item score carries no information and is dropped, as lavaan drops it.

Choosing fmi for a given missing_prop. The two are not the same number. The FMI of the coefficient depends on the number of items and how strongly they are correlated, because information lost on one item is partly recovered from the others; under data missing completely at random it is bounded by the largest rates of univariate and pairwise missingness (Savalei & Rhemtulla, 2012). For the population of the second example (four parallel items, reliability .80, width .15), missing_prop = .2 gives coefficient alpha and coefficient omega an FMI of .184 relative to every case, the footing of the planner's fmi (from one FIML fit to 200,000 simulated cases; it is .182 relative to the cases the fit keeps, since a share \(.2^4 = .0016\) of them loses every item). In 1,000 replications with the default ci_method = "ml" (set.seed(113) before each call), the complete data plan (\(N = 74\)) gave alpha intervals that averaged .153 wide with complete data and .170 with missing_prop = .2, wider by close to the width inflation factor \(1 / \sqrt{1 - .184} = 1.107\), while the plan made with fmi = .184 (\(N = 91\)) averaged .152 with missing_prop = .2. The help page of ss_aipe_reliability describes where a planning FMI comes from in practice.

The fraction of missing information the data realized. With missing_prop above 0, every replication that returns an interval also estimates the FMI of its coefficient from the same simulated data, as fraction_missing_information does with its default unstructured estimator: the FIML fit behind the coefficient is refit at its estimates with the information of the observed data and with the information complete data would have carried, and the FMI is one minus the ratio of the coefficient's complete data sampling variance to its sampling variance with the data as observed. For alpha the fit is the saturated model of the items whose covariance matrix the classical coefficient is computed from, and the three estimators of Chen and Savalei (2021) coincide for a saturated model (p. 9); for omega it is the single-factor model, and the FMI is that of its model implied coefficient. The FMI is taken relative to all n simulated cases, the N of the plan. A case that loses every item score is set aside by the fit, and the FMI relative to the \(n_{used}\) cases the fit used, \(\gamma_{used}\) (the FMI that fraction_missing_information reports), leaves out the information those cases would have carried; it is folded in as \(1 - (n_{used} / n)(1 - \gamma_{used})\). The difference matters with few items and much missing data: a share \(p^J\) of the cases loses every item, with p the value of missing_prop, which is .125 for three items at missing_prop = .5. The mean over the replications is the mean_realized_fmi attribute and is printed under the table, so the fmi a plan assumed can be read beside the FMI that the simulated missing data cost the coefficient. A single sample FMI is a poor guide: in the simulations of Chen and Savalei (2021, p. 9) the sample FMI of a regression coefficient was largely unbiased but varied from sample to sample, with root mean squared errors of about .10 or more at N = 50 and 100. The mean over many replications is the stable figure, and it is the value to carry into fmi for a study whose missing data the simulation mimics. A replication whose FMI cannot be computed (a fit that fails, or an improper solution that lavaan will not refit at its estimates; see fraction_missing_information) is left out of the mean, and the n_realized_fmi attribute counts the replications that entered it. The computation adds a model fit and two refits to every replication, about doubling the time a replication takes.

Bootstrap intervals. When ci_method is a bootstrap method ("bootstrap_se", "bootstrap_se_logistic", "percentile", or "bca"), every one of the G replications runs its own bootstrap of B resamples, so the simulation computes the coefficient \(G \times B\) times. The default B is the larger of 200 and one and a quarter times the number of replications the interval method and the level require (see dmar_bootstrap): at the 95 percent level, 500 for "percentile", 2500 for "bca", and 200 for the two bootstrap standard error methods. The quarter leaves room for replications that return no value: the number required is held to the request, so a simulated study that loses a few replications still reports its interval, and with the quarter its limits still rest on about the number required. That default is far below the B = 10000 of reliability_alpha and reliability_omega and keeps the product manageable. It also makes each replication's limits less precise than the reported interval's would be: a percentile limit at B = 500 rests on about 12 resamples in each tail, and the Monte Carlo error of the limits adds to the spread of the realized widths. A check of a bootstrap interval that will be reported with a large B is closer to that interval with a larger B here, at a cost that grows in proportion. A B below the required number is refused unless options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set; the run is then marked by one warning of class dmar_bootstrap_exploratory for the call, not one for each simulated study.

The omega coefficient. Omega is computed with denominator = "model_implied", the coefficient whose delta method interval the planner evaluates and the one the Wald intervals are defined for. For the parallel population simulated here the model implied and observed denominators estimate the same value.

Coverage at a true reliability of zero. Coverage and the misses in each tail are counted on the interval the estimation function reports, whose limits are each clamped into [0, 1] (see reliability_alpha), since that is the interval a plan is made for and a study reports. Clamping can only raise the coverage of a value in [0, 1], and at the boundary it does: with true_reliability = 0, an alpha interval lying wholly below zero is reported as [0, 0], which contains zero, so pct_ci_miss_high is zero by construction and total_type_I_error is the rate of misses low. A miss high there would place the reliability below zero, outside the range a reliability coefficient can take. With four items, \(N = 40\), and Bonett's interval (400 replications, set.seed(1)) the intervals miss .0075 of the time, all of it low. For any true reliability above zero, an interval lying wholly below zero misses high.

Replications that fail. A replication that returns no interval (a fit that did not converge, which is more common under full information maximum likelihood with small samples and much missing data, a fit whose likelihood has no maximum, which the estimation functions refuse with an error of class dmar_no_maximum when an error variance runs off below zero while the likelihood is flat or still rising, or an interval the method could not form) is set aside: it counts in no summary, and one warning states how many were set aside and the first reason. When no replication returns an interval, the function stops with that reason rather than return a table of missing values.

The record of the simulation

Every sensitivity function of the package summarizes its replications over one denominator: the replications that produced a confidence interval (for a power sensitivity function, a test). The proportion of intervals that met the width target (pct_ci_less_width), the proportions of intervals that missed the true value, and the summaries of the widths are all taken over those replications. A replication without an interval is in none of these rows. It is counted, and the returned table carries the counts in its attribute simulation, a list read with attr(x, "simulation"):

attempted

the number of replications asked for (G).

returned

the number that produced an interval (a test).

failed

the number that did not (attempted - returned).

denominator

the number of replications the rows named above are taken over, which is returned.

width_target_probability

the proportion of the replications with an interval whose interval met the width target, the value of the pct_ci_less_width row; NA for a function or a call without a width target, and when no replication produced an interval.

width_target_mc_ci

the exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) limits for that proportion, at the confidence level of the table. They describe the error of the simulation, which shrinks as G grows, and nothing else.

A function that records more about its run adds elements to the list, and its help page names them. The line "Replications" beneath the printed table gives G, and the three counts when a replication was without an interval. With many replications without an interval the rows describe only the studies in which the interval could be formed, so failed is to be reported beside them.

References

Bonett, D. G. (2002). Sample size requirements for testing and estimating coefficient alpha. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 27(4), 335–340. doi:10.3102/10769986027004335

Chen, L., & Savalei, V. (2021). Three sample estimates of fraction of missing information from full information maximum likelihood. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 667802. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2021.667802

Kelley, K., & Pornprasertmanit, S. (2016). Confidence intervals for population reliability coefficients: Evaluation of methods, recommendations, and software for composite measures. Psychological Methods, 21, 69–92. doi:10.1037/a0040086

Savalei, V., & Rhemtulla, M. (2012). On obtaining estimates of the fraction of missing information from full information maximum likelihood. Structural Equation Modeling, 19(3), 477–494. doi:10.1080/10705511.2012.687669

Terry, L. J., & Kelley, K. (2012). Sample size planning for composite reliability coefficients: Accuracy in parameter estimation via narrow confidence intervals. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 65, 371–401. doi:10.1111/j.2044-8317.2011.02030.x

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

van Zyl, J. M., Neudecker, H., & Nel, D. G. (2000). On the distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator of Cronbach's alpha. Psychometrika, 65(3), 271–280. doi:10.1007/BF02296146

Examples

# Reduced Monte Carlo sweep (small G) so the example runs quickly;
# raise G for a production sensitivity analysis.
set.seed(113)
ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(
  true_reliability     = 0.80,
  supposed_reliability = 0.80,
  n_items = 4, width = 0.15,
  estimator = "alpha",
  G = 20, print_iter = FALSE
)
#>  term                 value
#>  mean_reliability     0.782
#>  median_reliability   0.792
#>  sd_reliability       0.041
#>  mean_ci_width        0.163
#>  median_ci_width      0.155
#>  sd_ci_width          0.031
#>  pct_ci_less_width    0.450
#>  pct_ci_miss_low      0.000
#>  pct_ci_miss_high     0.050
#>  total_type_I_error   0.050
#>  total_N              74   
#>  n_items              4    
#>  true_reliability     0.800
#>  supposed_reliability 0.800
#>  width                0.150
#>  conf_level           0.950
#> 
#> Replications: 20
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The same plan made for an FMI of .18 and checked against data with each
# item score missing completely at random with probability .2, analyzed
# by full information maximum likelihood. The second line under the table
# gives the FMI those data realized for the coefficient, to read beside
# the .18 the plan assumed. Every replication fits a model, so G = 3 only
# shows the call; a reported check deserves G = 1000.
set.seed(113)
ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(
  true_reliability     = 0.80,
  supposed_reliability = 0.80,
  n_items = 4, width = 0.15,
  estimator = "alpha",
  G = 3, fmi = 0.18, missing_prop = 0.2
)
#>  term                 value
#>  mean_reliability     0.819
#>  median_reliability   0.830
#>  sd_reliability       0.030
#>  mean_ci_width        0.132
#>  median_ci_width      0.124
#>  sd_ci_width          0.023
#>  pct_ci_less_width    0.667
#>  pct_ci_miss_low      0.000
#>  pct_ci_miss_high     0.000
#>  total_type_I_error   0.000
#>  total_N              90   
#>  n_items              4    
#>  true_reliability     0.800
#>  supposed_reliability 0.800
#>  width                0.150
#>  conf_level           0.950
#> 
#> Replications: 3
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Planned for a fraction of missing information of 0.18; simulated with each item score missing completely at random with probability 0.2 and analyzed by full information maximum likelihood.
#> The fraction of missing information the simulated data realized for the coefficient averaged 0.156 over the 3 replications in which it was computed.
